title: Inscribing Changes — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, Transactions

subChunks.title: INSERT — Adding Rows
subChunks.hookHtml: SELECT reads. INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE write. The pattern matters because writes are permanent by default — a SELECT that returns the wrong rows is annoying, but a DELETE that targets the wrong rows is a recovery operation. Start with INSERT, the safest of the three.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Single-row INSERT — the explicit form

INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank, xp)
VALUES ('Eleanor', 'Novice', 0);

Two parts: (name, rank, xp) lists the columns you're providing values for. VALUES (...) lists the values in the same order.

Why list columns explicitly? Because the table might have other columns — a primary key id (auto-generated), a created_at timestamp (auto-defaulted) — that you want the database to fill in.

The dangerous shorthand — no column list

-- Works today but breaks tomorrow:
INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES (5, 'Eleanor', 'Novice', 0);

Without the column list, you must provide a value for every column in declaration order. Any later schema change — adding a new column, reordering — silently breaks every INSERT statement that uses this form. Always list columns explicitly in production code.

Multi-row INSERT

INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank, xp)
VALUES
  ('Eleanor', 'Novice', 0),
  ('Faelar',  'Novice', 0),
  ('Gareth',  'Novice', 0);

Most engines support comma-separated VALUES tuples. Roughly N times faster than running N separate INSERTs because there's only one round-trip and one transaction overhead.

INSERT ... SELECT

-- Copy rows from one table into another:
INSERT INTO archived_apprentices (id, name, rank, xp, archived_at)
SELECT id, name, rank, xp, NOW()
FROM apprentices
WHERE last_active < NOW() - INTERVAL '1 year';

Use the result of any SELECT as the source for an INSERT. Powerful for batch operations — archiving, denormalisation refreshes, ETL.

RETURNING — get back what was just inserted

PostgreSQL and a few other engines let you ask for the inserted row(s) back, including any auto-generated values:

INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank, xp)
VALUES ('Eleanor', 'Novice', 0)
RETURNING id, created_at;

Without RETURNING you'd need a separate SELECT after the INSERT, which is two round-trips and a race condition risk if other inserts happen in between.

What can go wrong

  • NOT NULL violation — you didn't supply a value for a NOT NULL column with no default
  • FK violation — you inserted a row whose foreign key points to a non-existent parent
  • Unique violation — the values would create a duplicate of a UNIQUE column or PK
  • CHECK violation — the values fail a CHECK constraint (e.g. xp >= 0)

Constraint violations are loud — the engine errors and rolls back the INSERT. They are not silent corruption. Embrace constraints; they are the database's way of catching bugs before bad data lands.

storyBeats.text: Cipher hands you the master quill — the one used for binding new entries into the ledgers. 'Up to now you have only read. Now you write.'

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Reading is reversible. Writing is not. Or rather: it is reversible only inside a transaction, which we will get to. But the default behaviour of an INSERT is permanent. The Headmaster has approved a new apprentice — Eleanor. Bind her into the ledger.

storyBeats.speaker: INSERT, two ways
storyBeats.text:
-- Best practice — name the columns explicitly:
INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank, xp)
VALUES ('Eleanor', 'Novice', 0);

-- Shorthand that bites you later:
INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES (5, 'Eleanor', 'Novice', 0);
-- Tomorrow someone adds a 'last_login' column.
-- This second statement now fails — wrong number of values.
-- Or worse: it shifts every value into the wrong column.
-- The first statement is unaffected by the schema change.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Always name your columns. Always. The cost is one extra line. The benefit is that your INSERT statement is robust against every future schema change. It is the cheapest discipline in SQL — and almost every junior I have trained has been bitten by ignoring it.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And don't fear constraint violations. NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK — these are the database refusing to accept inconsistent data. They are doing exactly the work you want. A constraint error is a bug caught early. The alternative — disabling constraints to avoid errors — is the path to a database full of garbage that nobody can clean up.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Bind three new apprentices into the ledger

The Headmaster has approved three new Novices: Eleanor, Faelar, and Gareth. All three start at 0 xp. Bind them into the apprentices ledger using a single multi-row INSERT with an explicit column list (no shorthand).

  • One INSERT statement, three VALUES tuples
  • Specify columns explicitly: (name, rank, xp)
  • The original four apprentices (Alice, Bjorn, Cassia, Dorian) must remain untouched
  • The id column auto-increments — don't supply it

Schema:

apprentices(
  id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  rank TEXT NOT NULL,
  xp   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
)
-- existing rows: Alice/Apprentice/1200, Bjorn/Adept/2400,
--                Cassia/Mage/4800, Dorian/Novice/80
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- Add Eleanor, Faelar, and Gareth as new Novices with 0 xp.
-- Single multi-row INSERT, explicit (name, rank, xp).

INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank, xp) VALUES
  -- ('Eleanor', ..., ...),
  -- ('Faelar',  ..., ...),
  -- ('Gareth',  ..., ...)
;

guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE apprentices (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, name TEXT NOT NULL, rank TEXT NOT NULL, xp INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0); INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank, xp) VALUES ('Alice','Apprentice',1200),('Bjorn','Adept',2400),('Cassia','Mage',4800),('Dorian','Novice',80);
guidedPracticeTests.verifyQuery: SELECT name FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice' AND xp = 0 ORDER BY name

guidedPracticeTests.label: Total apprentice count grows from 4 to 7
Original four apprentices unchanged
guidedPracticeTests.verifyQuery: SELECT name, rank, xp FROM apprentices WHERE id <= 4 ORDER BY id

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why the form `INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES ('Eleanor', 'Novice', 0);` (no column list) is a maintenance liability even when it works today. Walk through what happens when a teammate later adds a 'last_login' column.

questions.questionHtml: What's the safer form of INSERT for production code?
options: INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank, xp) VALUES ('Eleanor', 'Novice', 0);
INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES ('Eleanor', 'Novice', 0);
INSERT 'Eleanor', 'Novice', 0 INTO apprentices;
INSERT VALUES ('Eleanor', 'Novice', 0) INTO apprentices;
questions.correctAnswer: INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank, xp) VALUES ('Eleanor', 'Novice', 0);
questions.explanationHtml: Always list columns explicitly. The shorthand without a column list silently breaks (or worse, mis-fills) when the schema changes — adding a new column, reordering columns. The explicit form is robust.

questions.questionHtml: What does INSERT INTO apprentices_archive ... SELECT ... FROM apprentices WHERE ... do?
options: Copies the rows from one table into another in a single statement
Replaces every row in apprentices_archive with the SELECT's result
Defines a view called apprentices_archive
Creates a foreign-key relationship
questions.correctAnswer: Copies the rows from one table into another in a single statement
questions.explanationHtml: INSERT ... SELECT is the workhorse for batch copies — archiving, refreshing denormalised tables, ETL. The SELECT runs first, and its result rows are inserted into the target table.

questions.questionHtml: The schema is apprentices(id PK auto-generated, name TEXT NOT NULL, rank TEXT NOT NULL, xp INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0). Which of these statements succeeds without error?
options: INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank) VALUES ('Faelar', 'Novice');  -- xp defaults to 0
INSERT INTO apprentices (rank, xp) VALUES ('Novice', 0);  -- name omitted
INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES ('Faelar', 'Novice');  -- two values for four columns
INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank) VALUES ('Faelar', NULL);  -- rank is NOT NULL
questions.correctAnswer: INSERT INTO apprentices (name, rank) VALUES ('Faelar', 'Novice');  -- xp defaults to 0
questions.explanationHtml: Option 1 omits xp, which has a DEFAULT 0, so the engine fills it in. Option 2 omits the NOT NULL name column with no default — error. Option 3 supplies the wrong number of values for the implicit column list — error. Option 4 supplies NULL to a NOT NULL column — error.

questions.questionHtml: A teammate suggests "disabling foreign-key constraints during a bulk import to avoid errors." Why is this usually a bad idea?
options: Constraint errors signal bad data; suppressing them just allows inconsistent rows in, which then break every later query that joins through those FKs
FK constraints cannot be disabled in any modern SQL engine
Disabling constraints permanently corrupts the table
It would force the import to run in a single transaction
questions.correctAnswer: Constraint errors signal bad data; suppressing them just allows inconsistent rows in, which then break every later query that joins through those FKs
questions.explanationHtml: FK errors are the database telling you "this row references a parent that doesn't exist." Disabling the constraint doesn't fix the underlying problem — it just lets the inconsistent row in, where it'll cause silent join failures, mysteriously NULL-laden reports, and eventually a data-integrity emergency. The right fix is almost always to insert parents before children, or to use a transaction so partial imports roll back cleanly.

subChunks.title: UPDATE & DELETE — The Always-WHERE Rule
subChunks.hookHtml: The two most dangerous statements in SQL are UPDATE without a WHERE and DELETE without a WHERE. The first silently corrupts every row in a table. The second silently empties it. Both run quietly. Both have ended careers. Learn the discipline now: always WHERE, always preview, always be explicit.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
UPDATE — modifying existing rows

UPDATE apprentices
SET    rank = 'Adept',
       xp   = xp + 500
WHERE  id = 1;

Three parts: the table, the SET assignments, and the WHERE filter. Every row matching the WHERE has its columns updated to the SET values. Rows that don't match are unchanged.

Note xp = xp + 500 — you can reference a column's existing value on the right-hand side. The SET assignments all see the old values, not the partially-updated values, so this is well-defined.

The catastrophic UPDATE

-- Intent: bump Alice's xp
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 500;
--                                  ↑ no WHERE — every row is updated

This is the quintessential SQL disaster. There is no error, no warning, no "are you sure?" The query runs. Every apprentice's xp goes up by 500. Recovery requires backups, point-in-time restore, or rebuilding from logs.

Most production teams use a safe-update mode in their database client (MySQL has one built in) that refuses UPDATE/DELETE without a WHERE on a key column. Worth turning on locally too.

DELETE — removing rows

DELETE FROM apprentices
WHERE  rank = 'Novice' AND xp = 0;

Same shape: table, WHERE filter. Rows matching the WHERE are removed.

Same disaster mode: DELETE FROM apprentices; empties the table. Same prevention: always preview, always have a WHERE.

The preview habit

The single most valuable habit when writing UPDATE or DELETE: write the SELECT first.

-- Step 1: Confirm what rows you'd touch.
SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice' AND xp = 0;

-- Step 2: Eyeball the result. Is it the rows you intend?
--          If you see something unexpected, STOP.

-- Step 3: Convert SELECT to DELETE/UPDATE.
DELETE FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice' AND xp = 0;

Same WHERE clause, same row set. The preview catches WHERE-clause bugs before they're irreversible. This habit is non-negotiable in production database work.

UPDATE with a JOIN — engine-specific syntax

Sometimes you need to update one table based on values in another:

-- PostgreSQL form:
UPDATE apprentices a
SET    xp = a.xp + 100
FROM   recent_completions c
WHERE  c.apprentice_id = a.id;

-- MySQL form:
UPDATE apprentices a
JOIN   recent_completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
SET    a.xp = a.xp + 100;

Engine differences matter here. Check the manual for your database. The intent is identical — update rows in A based on a join with B.

Atomicity — multiple statements that must succeed together

UPDATE alone updates one table. What if you need to update two tables — "transfer 100 XP from Alice to Bjorn"? You need both UPDATEs to succeed, or both to fail (you don't want to debit Alice and forget to credit Bjorn). That's what transactions do — next sub-chunk.

storyBeats.text: Cipher's voice goes quiet. He sets the quill down deliberately.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Listen carefully. The two most dangerous statements I will teach you in this entire course are UPDATE without a WHERE, and DELETE without a WHERE. They run silently. They give no warning. They modify or destroy every row in the table. I have seen ten years of an institution's records vanish in under a second.

storyBeats.speaker: The catastrophe
storyBeats.text:
-- Intent: bump Alice's XP by 500.
-- Reality: the apprentice forgot the WHERE.
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 500;

-- Every apprentice's XP just went up by 500.
-- Recovery: backups, audit logs, careful reconstruction.
-- Time required: hours to days.
-- Time required to PREVENT it: writing 'WHERE id = 1'.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: There is one habit that separates senior database hands from juniors, and it is this: write the SELECT first. Same WHERE clause. Look at the rows that come back. Are they the rows you intended? If yes, swap SELECT for DELETE or UPDATE. If anything looks off — anything at all — stop and re-examine. The preview catches almost every WHERE-clause bug before it lands.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And one more. When you must run an UPDATE or DELETE on production data, run it inside a transaction first. BEGIN; UPDATE ...; SELECT ...; — verify the result before COMMIT;. If anything looks wrong, ROLLBACK; and nothing changed. We will cover transactions next. They are how you make irreversible operations reversible until you say otherwise.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Trace each modification

Predict what each statement does to the apprentices table. Several are intentionally dangerous — identify them.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a junior the 'always SELECT first' habit when writing UPDATE or DELETE. Walk through one concrete scenario where the preview would have saved them from a production-data disaster.

questions.questionHtml: What does UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 500; do?
options: Updates every row in the apprentices table — adds 500 to each one's xp
Updates only the first row matching xp = xp + 500
Errors out — UPDATE requires a WHERE clause
Returns a list of rows where xp + 500 would be valid
questions.correctAnswer: Updates every row in the apprentices table — adds 500 to each one's xp
questions.explanationHtml: Without a WHERE, every row matches and is updated. The engine does not require WHERE — it assumes "no filter" means "all rows." This is the canonical SQL disaster.

questions.questionHtml: You want to delete only the Novice apprentices with zero XP. Which statement is correct AND safe?
options: First run SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice' AND xp = 0; verify the result is what you intend; then run DELETE FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice' AND xp = 0;
DELETE FROM apprentices; -- and rely on quick reflexes if it looks wrong
DELETE FROM apprentices WHERE rank IS NOT NULL;
TRUNCATE apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice';
questions.correctAnswer: First run SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice' AND xp = 0; verify the result is what you intend; then run DELETE FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Novice' AND xp = 0;
questions.explanationHtml: The preview-as-SELECT-first habit. Same WHERE, you see the rows you'd delete, you eyeball them, then you swap SELECT for DELETE. Option 2 deletes everything. Option 3's WHERE matches almost every row (Novice or not, as long as rank isn't NULL). Option 4 isn't valid SQL — TRUNCATE doesn't take a WHERE clause; it empties whole tables.

questions.questionHtml: In UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100 WHERE id = 1;, what does the right-hand xp refer to?
options: The current (pre-update) value of xp for that row
The new (post-update) value of xp for that row
The xp value of a different table called xp
Always 0 — column references on the right-hand side default to 0
questions.correctAnswer: The current (pre-update) value of xp for that row
questions.explanationHtml: Right-hand-side column references in SET see the row's existing values. So xp = xp + 100 reads the current xp, adds 100, and stores the result. All SET expressions see the same pre-update snapshot, so updates that mutually reference each other are well-defined.

questions.questionHtml: A junior is debugging a query and runs DELETE FROM apprentices WHERE name = 'Eleanor';. Nobody named Eleanor exists. What happens?
options: Zero rows are deleted; the statement succeeds with a 'rows affected: 0' message and no error
All rows in the table are deleted because the WHERE matches nothing
The engine throws an error because no rows match
The engine prompts for confirmation
questions.correctAnswer: Zero rows are deleted; the statement succeeds with a 'rows affected: 0' message and no error
questions.explanationHtml: A WHERE that matches no rows is not an error — it's a successful statement that affected zero rows. This is one reason why "the DELETE succeeded" is not the same as "the DELETE did what you intended." Always check the rows-affected count and ideally use the SELECT-first habit to confirm the row set before running.

subChunks.title: Transactions — All or Nothing
subChunks.hookHtml: A transfer of 100 XP from Alice to Bjorn is two UPDATEs — minus 100 from Alice, plus 100 to Bjorn. If the second one fails, you've debited Alice without crediting Bjorn — money lost from the system. Transactions are how you bundle multiple statements into an all-or-nothing unit. BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK — three keywords that turn SQL from a sequence of risks into a reliable system of record.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The shape of a transaction

BEGIN;
  UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp - 100 WHERE id = 1;  -- Alice
  UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100 WHERE id = 2;  -- Bjorn
COMMIT;

BEGIN opens a transaction. The two UPDATEs happen tentatively — visible only to the current connection until COMMIT. COMMIT publishes them atomically: either both succeed and become permanent together, or neither does.

If the second UPDATE failed, the application could call ROLLBACK instead, and both UPDATEs would be undone as if they never happened.

Auto-commit — the default mode

Most database connections run in auto-commit mode: every individual statement is implicitly wrapped in BEGIN; ...; COMMIT;. You don't see the BEGIN/COMMIT, but they're there. To group statements, you turn off auto-commit (or explicitly begin a transaction) and write COMMIT yourself.

Different clients handle this differently:

  • psql (PostgreSQL CLI): auto-commit on by default; BEGIN turns it off until COMMIT/ROLLBACK
  • JDBC / Java: connection.setAutoCommit(false), then connection.commit() or connection.rollback()
  • Spring: @Transactional annotation does the BEGIN/COMMIT around your method body

ACID — what transactions guarantee

LetterMeaning
AtomicityAll statements in a transaction succeed together or none do
ConsistencyThe database's invariants (constraints, triggers) hold before and after
IsolationConcurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted state
DurabilityOnce COMMIT returns, the data survives crashes

Atomicity is the most relevant on day one. Isolation gets interesting when many users hit the database at once (different isolation levels offer different trade-offs — covered in advanced material). Durability is what makes "the database is the source of truth."

SAVEPOINT — partial rollback

BEGIN;
  INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES (...);
  SAVEPOINT before_lines;
  INSERT INTO order_lines (...) VALUES (...);   -- this fails
  ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_lines;            -- undo just the lines
  -- order is still there; can try a different INSERT
COMMIT;

SAVEPOINT lets you undo to a specific point inside a transaction without rolling back the whole thing. Useful for batch operations where individual items may fail but you want to keep the successes.

Idempotency — write statements that are safe to retry

If your application retries a transaction after a transient failure (network blip, deadlock retry), make sure each statement is safe to apply once or many times.

-- Idempotent — fine to retry:
UPDATE apprentices SET rank = 'Adept' WHERE id = 1;

-- NOT idempotent — retry doubles the increment:
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100 WHERE id = 1;

-- Made idempotent with a guard:
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100
WHERE id = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM xp_audit
  WHERE apprentice_id = 1 AND idempotency_key = 'transfer-2026-04-30-abc'
);
INSERT INTO xp_audit (apprentice_id, idempotency_key) VALUES (1, 'transfer-...');

The pattern: pair the increment with an audit row using a unique key. The retry sees the audit row and skips the increment. This is how production payment systems handle retries.

The discipline

  1. Anything that touches more than one row or table → wrap in a transaction
  2. Anything you want to undo → run inside a transaction and ROLLBACK
  3. Anything that might be retried → make it idempotent

storyBeats.text: Cipher draws a small box on the parchment, with two arrows entering and one arrow leaving.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The Headmaster wants 100 XP transferred from Alice to Bjorn. Two updates: one debit, one credit. If only the debit succeeds, XP has vanished from the system. If only the credit succeeds, XP appeared from nowhere. Both must happen, or neither must happen. This all-or-nothing guarantee is the entire purpose of a transaction.

storyBeats.speaker: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Atomicity is the headline guarantee. The acronym is ACID — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. The other three matter, especially when many users use the database at once. But in your first year of database work, atomicity is the one that turns SQL from 'a sequence of risks' into 'a reliable system.' Use transactions whenever you touch more than one row or more than one table.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And remember: applications retry. Networks blip, deadlocks happen, the system tries again. Make your statements idempotent — safe to apply once or many times. UPDATE xp = xp + 100 is not idempotent — a retry doubles the credit. The fix is an audit row with a unique key, and a guard that skips if the audit row already exists. Production payment systems live and die by this discipline.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Reason about the transaction

For each block, identify what state the database ends in. Pay attention to which blocks COMMIT vs ROLLBACK.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a junior why an XP transfer between two apprentices must run inside a transaction. What goes wrong if the two UPDATEs run as separate auto-committed statements and the connection drops between them?

questions.questionHtml: What does the A in ACID stand for, and what does it guarantee?
options: Atomicity — all statements in a transaction succeed together, or none do
Aliasing — every column gets a unique name
Authentication — only logged-in users can run transactions
Asynchrony — transactions don't block each other
questions.correctAnswer: Atomicity — all statements in a transaction succeed together, or none do
questions.explanationHtml: Atomicity is the all-or-nothing guarantee. C is Consistency (constraints hold), I is Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's in-progress state), D is Durability (committed data survives crashes).

questions.questionHtml:
You run this in a fresh psql session:

BEGIN;
  UPDATE apprentices SET xp = 0 WHERE id = 1;
  -- you decide this was wrong
ROLLBACK;

What is the state of apprentice id=1 after ROLLBACK?
options: Unchanged — the UPDATE never became permanent because the transaction was rolled back
xp = 0 — the UPDATE was permanent before ROLLBACK ran
Half-updated — ROLLBACK only undoes the most recent statement
The row is deleted
questions.correctAnswer: Unchanged — the UPDATE never became permanent because the transaction was rolled back
questions.explanationHtml: Inside a transaction, statements are tentative until COMMIT. ROLLBACK undoes everything since BEGIN. Other connections never even saw the UPDATE happen — only this connection's queries within the transaction did.

questions.questionHtml: Which UPDATE is idempotent — safe to apply more than once?
options: UPDATE apprentices SET rank = 'Adept' WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp + 100 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp * 2 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE apprentices SET xp = xp - 50 WHERE id = 1;
questions.correctAnswer: UPDATE apprentices SET rank = 'Adept' WHERE id = 1;
questions.explanationHtml: Setting rank to a literal value is idempotent — applying it twice gives the same result as applying it once. Increment/decrement/multiply update statements are NOT idempotent — running them twice doubles the effect. To make them idempotent, pair them with an audit row keyed by a unique idempotency key.

questions.questionHtml: A teammate writes a script that runs five UPDATEs to update five rows in different tables, no transaction. The third UPDATE fails halfway. What's the state of the database afterwards?
options: Inconsistent — UPDATEs 1 and 2 are permanent, 3 failed, 4 and 5 never ran. The database is in a partially-updated state and recovery requires manual surgery
Atomic — the failure rolled back UPDATEs 1 and 2 automatically
Atomic — all five UPDATEs ran because the engine retries failures
Identical to the start state — failed scripts always undo their changes
questions.correctAnswer: Inconsistent — UPDATEs 1 and 2 are permanent, 3 failed, 4 and 5 never ran. The database is in a partially-updated state and recovery requires manual surgery
questions.explanationHtml: Without an explicit transaction, each UPDATE is its own auto-committed transaction. They are independent. If the third one fails, the first two are already permanent and the last two never run. This is exactly the failure mode that transactions exist to prevent. Wrap multi-statement work in BEGIN ... COMMIT to make it atomic.
